question_text: A previously healthy 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of increasing visual loss and deterioration of his hearing and speech over the past 2 months. During this period, he has had difficulty walking, using the stairs, and feeding himself. His teachers have noticed that he has had difficulty concentrating. His grades have worsened and his handwriting has become illegible. His maternal male cousin had similar complaints and died at the age of 6 years. Vital signs are within normal limits. Examination shows hyperpigmented skin and nails and an ataxic gait. His speech is dysarthric. Neurologic examination shows spasticity and decreased muscle strength in all extremities. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally. Plantar reflex shows an extensor response bilaterally. Sensation is decreased in the lower extremities. Fundoscopy shows optic atrophy. There is sensorineural hearing loss bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

                    ### Question
                    A previously healthy 8-year-old boy is brought to the physician because of increasing visual loss and deterioration of his hearing and speech over the past 2 months. Deep tendon reflexes are 4+ bilaterally. Plantar reflex shows an extensor response bilaterally. Sensation is decreased in the lower extremities. Fundoscopy shows optic atrophy. There is sensorineural hearing loss bilaterally. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms?

                    ### Options
                    opa. β-Glucocerebrosidase deficiency
opb. ATP-binding cassette transporter dysfunction
opc. Arylsulfatase A deficiency

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The clinical presentation of the 8-year-old boy, including progressive visual loss, hearing deterioration, ataxia, dysarthria, spasticity, and hyperpigmented skin, suggests a lysosomal storage disorder. The family history of similar symptoms in a maternal cousin further supports a genetic etiology. Among the options, Arylsulfatase A deficiency (associated with metachromatic leukodystrophy) is consistent with the neurological decline and hyperpigmentation observed. Other options, such as β-Glucocerebrosidase deficiency (Gaucher disease), ATP-binding cassette transporter dysfunction, and α-Galactosidase A deficiency (Fabry disease), are less likely due to the specific symptom profile and lack of hyperpigmentation. Lysosomal galactocerebrosidase deficiency (Krabbe disease) could also be considered, but the combination of symptoms aligns more closely with Arylsulfatase A deficiency. Therefore, the most likely cause of this patient's symptoms is Arylsulfatase A deficiency.
